utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We start a bit late. It is partly due to technical problems with the computer system, but also partly due to the late arrival of a witness. If the Prosecution could manage that the witnesses appear on time in the morning - because the last couple of minutes we had to wait for the witness - this would be highly appreciated by the Chamber. Since we had no procedural issues to discuss, we just can start right away with the witness. Your next witness, you call, Mr. Ierace, is?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Major General Abdel-Razek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, could you please escort -- yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would just like to tell the Chamber that it was half an hour ago that I was given a supplemental information sheet regarding the -- an interview which was conducted with Major General Abdel-Razek, but it was not in B/C/S so I was not able to tell General Galic about it. So perhaps I was not able to really get ready for this. Perhaps the learned colleagues can tell us when exactly we can get the translation, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a procedural issue. I think you were asked whether there were any procedural issues, and there were not. I take it that Mr. Ierace will inform you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Abdel-Razek, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. God may be my witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Abdel-Razek. Please be seated. May I ask the interpreter also to stand up since you are supposed to make the solemn declaration as well. I take it, Madam Registrar, do we have all the personal data of the interpreter? If not, can you please tell us your name and then make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: My name is Sabri, and I solemnly declare that I will independently and impartially, and with full respect for the duty of confidentiality, make my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. In the booth, we have difficulties of seeing who is exactly in the booth, but we hear a new voice, and since another language is involved, may I take it that all the interpreters in the booth, also the new ones, have made the solemn declaration before they started working in the booth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your information. Mr. Ierace, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is your full name Hussein Ali Abdel-Razek?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 3rd of July, 1944, in Egypt?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you graduate from the military academy in 1966?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over your military career, have you served variously as a platoon commander, company commander, battalion commander, brigade commander and division commander?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you also served in combat in the 1967 war, the war of attrition and the 1973 war, all in the Middle East?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- have you also served in various UN missions over the years?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Just in Angola and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, in terms of Sarajevo, were -- did you serve as Sector Commander in Sarajevo from the 21st of August, 1992, to the 20th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you replace Major General MacKenzie as Sarajevo Sector commander?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I heard you say "yes," but that wasn't caught by the transcript. Now it is.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the structure of Sector Sarajevo, were there three military battalions, being a French battalion commanded by Colonel Sartre, a Ukrainian Battalion and an Egyptian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the strength of each battalion around 500 to 600?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your staff include as one of your special political advisors, Mr. Mik Magnusson?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: The staff changed routinely. Mik Magnusson worked for me for a while. Fred Eckhart [phoen], also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if we could briefly go into closed session. I think it will save time, ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will turn into closed session and, therefore, unfortunately I have to ask those who are in the public gallery to leave for one second. Yes, I know, but, nevertheless it is a matter which has got hardly anything to do with his witness, but it is a procedural issue we have to discuss in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are in open session, so that also means that the public gallery is open again. We will just wait until the -- those who want to attend this hearing have had an opportunity to resume their seats. Since that has been taken care of, please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in terms of the daily functioning of your office and indeed the senior command levels of UNPROFOR, were there any daily meetings?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: The normal daily routine within UN command: A sector commander briefing meeting takes place at 7.00 in the morning. The meeting takes about half an hour, during which we review the situation that evolved the day before and also the intended plans for the same day. We would also discuss any obstacles that stood in the way of implementing the daily work, and then accordingly, I would give my instructions to the staff officers. This is the daily routine followed every day, every morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the meeting attendees include the senior military officer -- I am sorry, the senior military observer?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. The senior observer habitually attended the meeting with the staff officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you arrived in Sarajevo, was there any activity in the city in the form of shooting and the landing of artillery and mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: At the beginning, there were no sounds, there were no skirmishes, there was no combat, in fact. But I was told that there was a skirmish in the morning of my arrival and a Ukrainian soldier was shot dead during that skirmish. But when I was sitting in my office, I could hear rounds being fired. And I remember that I was talking to my deputy at that time and I said to him, "This is my welcome ceremony."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, during the time that you were in Sarajevo, was there ever a day when you did not hear the sound of shooting and shells impacting in the city?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The fighting was not daily, did not take place daily. They were intermittent. Sometimes they were very extensive. Sometimes they were on a much lower scale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your responsibilities, did you meet with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you do that during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: We met on several occasions, and when there was a host of problems or problems multiplied, we met on regular basis, to the point where we would agree that we would meet once a week. That is what exactly happened, but because of our schedules, we could not maintain the same rhythm of meetings and we only met when the situation necessitated such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often was that? In other words, how often did you actually meet him?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: We met every 10 days, every 15 days. There were times where we would not meet for 20 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Where would you have those meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: We met at his headquarters in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you typically take any staff with you to those meetings?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I was keen at all times to be accompanied by my deputy and the Chief of Staff of the sector and the civil affairs advisor, and sometimes I was accompanied by a representative of UNHCR, when there is an issue that related to the work of UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever accompanied to those meetings by Colonel Sartre?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Sartre came on occasions. Primarily, he was in charge of the coordination of the trips to and back from headquarters. He coordinated the security situation, the security arrangements with the various parties, and at times he accompanied me when there is or there were issues relating to the work of his battalion in the sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you have the assistance of an interpreter or interpreters when you met with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Interpreters always were provided by General Galic. If my memory serves me right, there were two girls who alternated on the interpretation Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. work, and I must admit their work was good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "their work was good," do you mean that the quality of their interpreting, as far as you knew, was good?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I believed that the interpretation was sufficient and conveyed the message that I wanted to get to him. And their interpretation of what he said gave me the impression that what he was saying was in the context of the issues we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have -- I withdraw that. Did you ever make any protests to General Galic in relation to the activities of his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. This was often the case. I always said to him, "Last night was a difficult night for all of us. We spent most of the time last night in bunkers." Then we moved on to discuss other issues that we needed to raise with Galic and his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the way your answer was interpreted was: "I always said to him, 'Last night was a difficult night for all of us.'" Did you mean "always" or did you mean "once," or something else?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: When I meet him, that is -- I say, I am using that as an example, but that is not always the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. All right. Staying with that example, why did you spend most of the previous night in a bunker, and whereabouts was that bunker?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: In the PTT building there are underground floors, and we used one of these floors as a bunker, as a shelter, when there were skirmishes, when there was fighting, and we felt the building might be affected as a result of the fighting. A siren sounded and we all hurried to the lower floor. We spent long hours in that shelter. We did not return to our offices, to our usual places, until the fighting has died down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The PTT building at that stage was the UN headquarters and included your office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Galic ever explain to you why he was, through his subordinates, shelling near or at the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: At the start, there was a denial of the fact that his forces were responsible for the shelling. He always said that is the other side, the other party, who was doing the shelling and were trying to implicate us in the process of the shelling. But when I reviewed the reports coming from the checkpoints, and most of these reports are within -- at the disposal of the UN, these reports showed clearly that the shelling came from the Serbian forces, the Serb forces. And when I insisted on stopping the shelling, he said to me: "You allow the other side to fire from the side, from the perimeter of the PTT building, and when we respond, some of the rounds might fall close to the PTT building." He said to me, "It is your responsibility to stop the other party, the other side, to stop the shelling." That is the way he dealt with us when it came to discussing the shelling. I personally took the matter upon myself and discussed the issue with the Bosnian side, and I said to them that if they did not stop such acts, which actually took place at the beginning of my term, then we would take the appropriate measures in this regard, and that we were going to tell press and the media about what was actually happening. As a result of that, they stopped. However, the PTT building was the target of shelling every now and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean after the firing by the Bosnians stopped, every now and then shells would still land on or near the building from the side controlled by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, without going into too much detail, was there an incident involving your secretary?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, my secretary was having a break. And the shelling took place on the building, and I was told that my secretary was affected and she was evacuated to the headquarters hospital. I went to see her, and the doctor recommended that she should be evacuated to a specialised hospital specialising in nerves or neurology. And we made sure that she was evacuated and sent to Zagreb the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts on the building did that shell land?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: It landed on the roof, on the roof of the building. And the shrapnel went to the other floors where the girls used to live. And unfortunately, my secretary was there and she was wounded or affected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of your secretary?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: She was Serb. I used to have two secretaries working with me; both of them were Serbs, and they were the best members of my staff. They used to cooperate with me and give me a great deal of help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Galic ever justify shelling the PTT building by claiming there was a munitions factory in it?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I do not recall that sir. However, as I was describing to you, I know the building perfectly well and I used to tour the building every hour. I did not see -- I have not received any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that you took refuge from the shelling in the underground floors. Did that involve you passing through the basement or did that, indeed, include the basement?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: The basement was the shelter in itself. It was sort of many floors, the lowest part of the building. So there were floors on the ground level and some below the ground level. So the underground level or floors, those floors, one of them, was used by the communication unit and it was serviced by a Dutch company. And this other floor was occupied by the medical unit and this was a French company. Another floor was divided in two parts: One for the soldiers brigade servicing the service unit, and the second part of the building or the floor was used by us as a shelter. And there used to be an office for the commander of the sector, equipped with the communication tools and equipments for such purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: There is yet another external part which was used as a parking lot for the United Nations cars and vehicles. Because as you know, the building was large.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone ever suggest to you -- I withdraw that. In any conversation you had when you were in Sarajevo, did anyone ever suggest to you that there was a munitions factory somewhere in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I do not recall that, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Coming back to the protests that you made to General Galic, you have told us now about your protests to do with the shelling of and near the PTT building. What else, if anything, did you protest to him about during your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: There were several issues, obviously. I do recall, for instance, that there were some obstacles erected by his forces on the roads. On the road to the airport, they used to erect barriers because, as you are aware, the main mandate of the United Nations in Sarajevo was to protect the airport so that it can function properly. So our activities are from the headquarters to the airport. So I put this matter to Galic. This took some time so that he can change his opinion or idea about this container.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can I interrupt you there? Did any of your protests to General Galic over the time you were in Sarajevo involve civilian casualties, the topic of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: As a commander of the United Nations forces, I received reports on the casualties from the mass media and through also the reports, the reports that we received from official quarters. I used to talk about this issue to him. I used to tell him that there are heavy losses among civilians, in addition to the fact that we were hindered in our work as a United Nations, we were not able to operate. And we incurred losses also as a UN. So I used to talk to him in this way concerning the shelling incidents. I also talked to him about the shelling of the hospital, and many other similar issues. We used to talk in a general way. There was shelling incident on the city. This shelling affected the civilian population and it does also impact on our work a great deal. And many times, on many occasions, we were not able to communicate and to communicate with other units of the United Nations, either from the PTT building or in another battalion, in the various camps of the battalions, Tito Barracks, for example, and the Egyptian Battalion. I don't quite recall the other names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you protest to him about the shelling of the city?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact figure, sir. But I do believe in many meetings we had, I did raise this issue. I used to raise this issue as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to the shelling of the hospital. Which hospital was that?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: The main hospital in the city. I don't remember the name of the hospital. A great deal of time has elapsed since then. But I believe that during the Secretary-General visit to the Sarajevo Sector and as a result of the various letters and reports that we've received, the Secretary-General asked to visit the hospital then, and he did actually visit the hospital. And he noticed how the hospital was affected and he listened to the problem -- various reports on the problems of the electricity cut. It was a highly complicated issue, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As best as you can recollect, how many hospitals were there in the city?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I do apologise. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was General Galic's response to you when you complained about the shelling of the city?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: General Galic sometimes used to deny the shelling incident. He denied the fact that his forces were responsible for the shelling incidents. And he used to say that they -- the other party did that. He used to say that they did that in order to attract the support of the international community, and sympathy. I should like to say here that that was the response I used to get from all parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear, while you were in Sarajevo, of any investigation by UN forces which found that the source of fire for a shelling incident in the city was also in the city? In other words, as far as you know, was there ever a UN investigation which established that Bosnian civilians were shelled by Bosnian forces?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I used to hear this from the Serb party only. However, in my meetings with the staff, we used to monitor the various reports emanating from the military observers. Those reports clarified from where the fire came. And you can go back to these reports because we used to send these reports to the command in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "Those reports clarified from where the fire came," in terms of the shelling of the city, what did those reports indicate as the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: They pointed to the fact that the fire -- most of the fire came from the party where the Serb troops were positioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Galic ever discuss the shelling of the city with you as a possible option or as a possible course open to him?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I apologise. The question was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you protested to General Galic about the city being shelled. Did he ever raise the shelling of the city with you in any context as a possible future course of action that he might take?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: He stated in a clear fashion that the other party -- if the other party continued in firing his troops or against his troops, he shall continue in attacking them. I do recall quite clearly that he said, during one of those meetings I had with him, he said, "I shall make them live difficult times." And I told him then, "But we are there, and we are also suffering from this." Can you imagine that I was unable to move my troops because of this shelling, and from time to time, I used to send reports containing information about losses incurred. So I told him that this shelling was painful and did have a great deal of effects, and the shelling does not help in any way in maintaining stability in the sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier the special responsibility that the UN had for the airport. Did you ever receive any reports of civilian casualties in the area of the airport?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: This area was an area that witnessed intensive firing activities, an exchange of fire, and the French Battalion actually was -- incurred a great deal of casualties. Civilians also were crossing the runway from Butmir to the city and vice versa. Some of the civilians were killed; some were injured and wounded as a result of the firing activities from the Serb party. I did raise this issue with General Galic, and on many Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. occasions I asked Mr. Sartre to contact him in order to discuss this matter with him. And this issue was a source of friction and tension. And people, because of their difficulties, they used to take great deal of risk in order to go and see their families, to be reunited with their family members. So a great deal of casualties did occur when they used to go through those roads, despite all our efforts to reduce this tension. But from time to time, we used to hear reports saying that civilians continued crossing those roads. And every day we received reports, telling us that a lady was killed with her child while she was trying to cross, and sometimes three bodies were discovered in one given place. And many casualties took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever protest yourself to General Galic about civilians being shot as they crossed the airfield by his forces?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk about this with him. And he was adamant on the fact that he will continue to stop this movement by all means, using all means. And he said the other party should put an end to these activities, and apparently he did have some doubt as to those movements. They might be for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when did those conversations take place with General Galic? I appreciate it is a long time ago. Perhaps your memory will allow you to indicate whether they were towards the beginning of your time there or in the middle or in the end, or in some similar fashion you could assist us?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I believe that it was close to my departure time, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to -- I withdraw that. Was it one conversation or more than one conversation where he gave that response to your protest about the shooting of civilians at the airport?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I believe that I have talked to him once about this specific issue. However, I did delegate the authority to the head of the French Battalion, delegate the authority to discuss this issue with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I will leave it at that point for now. Now, while you were in Sarajevo, did you notice whether, as far as you could determine, civilians were driving their cars, in other words, civilian cars?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: When times were quiet, there were movements. Cars were used and bicycles also were used. And then when things were quiet and calm, life seemed ordinary and natural. We used to meet with people going in the streets, taking their cars or taking their bicycles, and these things were changed only by the shelling incidents that took place from time to time. And as I said previously, skirmishes did not take place all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where, if you know, did civilians obtain fuel for their cars?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Obviously, they used to have oil in the city. I recall some of them told me that in the Holiday Inn they had a great deal of reserves of fuel. However, I don't know exactly how they used to manage this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any reports to you of a black market in fuel in Sarajevo operating during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there was an issue within the UN and I knew that armed vehicles, the BTR used by the Ukrainian Battalion, they -- they used to sell fuel outside Sarajevo when they used to go in order to secure the caravans of relief and to protect the relief convoys. They used to buy other things in order to sell them. It was something which was not quite normal and is outside the realm of discipline. In that specific battalion, we used to have problems. Some were accused, some of the people in that battalion, were accused of having stolen a car. Therefore, I set up an inquiry commission and I found out that the deputy of that battalion was involved in all these issues. And I recommended that he should be repatriated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the oil was only sold outside Sarajevo or whether it was sold inside Sarajevo as well?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Outside Sarajevo, as far as I recall. I should like to clarify one point here. Fuel used by tanks cannot be used by cars or vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is an aspect of this witness's evidence that I think should be given in closed session. I imagine it will take in the order of 10 minutes. So perhaps it will take us through to the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will then into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will have a break until 11.00. And could someone take care that those who were in the public gallery will also be informed that we are in open session again and that we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, now really, to everyone. Glad to see that you are there, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this morning I asked you whether General Galic ever raised in his meetings with you the shelling of the city as a possible future course of action that he might take. You replied as follows: "He stated in a clear fashion that the other party -- if the other party continued in firing his troops or against his troops, he shall continue in attacking them. I do recall quite clearly that he said, during one of those meetings I had with him, he said, 'I shall make them live difficult times.'" At least in the translation, that answer is open to a reference by General Galic to attacking the Bosnian government forces rather than shelling the city. Can you assist us further as to what it was that General Galic said?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: He was not specific about who he was going to shell. He said, "I am going to attack them, I am going to hit them," but he was not specific about who he was going to attack. But when we have shells landing next to us, there is all likelihood that they would land on the PTT building, on military positions, and on civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that he said: "I shall make them live difficult times"? Towards the beginning, the middle or the end of your tenure?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: When I started my job, the situation was extremely difficult. The three months -- the first three months of my tenure were extremely difficult. And I travelled between the Bosnian and Serb headquarters, and I was trying at the same time to calm the situation and prevent any danger from afflicting the civilians. I have to admit the first three months were extremely difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you when it was approximately that General Galic said to you the words, "I shall make them live difficult times"?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I cannot really exactly remember when these things were said. When I spoke about the difficult times and difficult situation started with the beginning of my tenure, beginning of my term, around August, September, October, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. When you travelled to Lukavica, did you notice whether or not there was any artillery or any mortars in place in the complex? By "in place," I mean ready to fire.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: On route to Lukavica, it was very easy to cross the road leading to the airport into Lukavica. It was very easy, even to a layman, to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. realise there were mortars, there were tanks, there were armoured vehicles. And in Lukavica proper, we visited some of the points where observers operated on the Serb side and that was during the trip conducted by Mr. Golding. I accompanied him in a visit to some of the posts to see where the observers were, how they operated, and all these posts that we visited were in the perimeter of Lukavica. It was abundantly clear to us that there was artillery positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can I interrupt you there. At any of the meetings that you had with General Galic, were there politicians present?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: In some of the meetings there was one man, the status of whom I did not know. He attended these meetings on a regular basis. Other meetings were attended by Ms. Plavsic. There were other meetings with the presence of UN leadership: Mr. Golding, General Nambiar, and other top UN officials. I used to accompany these individuals to the Serb command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have told us that Mrs. Plavsic was present with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: In some of the meetings, yes, she was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see General Galic present with Dr. Karadzic or any other political Serb leader?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is leading. Names are being quoted and so on, and perhaps the General's memory is being forced here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase the question in such a way that it is in a more general way put to the witness, whether one of the political -- those belonging to the political leadership would have been present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from Mrs. Plavsic, do you recall any other meetings that you attended where there were present General Galic and senior Serb political leaders?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Most of my meetings were of military nature. However, there was a person, an individual, who was present there all the time, the status of whom I do not know. I did not ask him who he was, what his position was, but he was there with us all the time. That person was there, and as I said, the status of whom I do not know, I am not aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned your last meeting with General Galic was at Pale. Where was your second last meeting with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: In Lukavica, I think. The only other time that I met General Galic in Pale was when I was going to say good-bye. I met him with the Prime Minister, Dr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you questions about the second last meeting. Was anything said at the second last meeting on the topic of civilians being shelled or shot in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I cannot exactly remember the items that were on the agenda at that meeting. However, every time I met General Galic, I raised the questions relating to the difficulties that we are confronting. I said that we were coming under pressure from the other side and has been hindering our movement and our work. These were the points that were raised in every meeting, practically. I cannot really pinpoint at what meeting what points were raised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, was there any meeting that you had at Lukavica at any time during which artillery or mortars, or both, were being fired in close proximity to your meeting place?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. There were occasions when this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any occasion when that happened that you said something to General Galic about it?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: As a military man, I understood that there were forces engaged at the time and I said to him, "That's an example of the situation that we had to live under in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving the opportunity to the Defence to cross-examine the witness, has the matter been solved to which was raised by Ms. Pilipovic at the beginning of the testimony of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have spoken to Mr. Piletta-Zanin about that. I have explained that the changes were made last night and that the supplemental information sheet was available for the first time this morning. I have also assisted Mr. Piletta-Zanin by pointing out the one change, I think, is of significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is more or less true, although I have to say that I did not receive the information yesterday which would have allowed me to look at it more closely. And now General Galic has still not been able to see what this is all about since, even if it is according to the Prosecution there is only one modification, important modification has to be done, the Defence has not had time to read it, on one hand, not even in English, and obviously not in Serbian. And there are certain things that only General Galic knows. And therefore, we are really -- it is impossible for us technically to proceed with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecution would need to give us a written translation. I don't know how long they would need to have this done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much text are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four pages. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I respectfully submit that I think it appropriate that Your Honours be aware of what the changes in order to make a proper assessment of how much time is really needed. There are four pages of text, it is true, but that text includes quotes from the original information sheet followed by the passage, in many cases one word changed, and in some cases, changed from the singular to the plural. The changes, I would respectfully submit, could be brought to the General's attention in a ten-minute conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I take it that you would not agree that ten minutes would be enough or did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a question, right. It would be sufficient, Mr. President, to inform General Galic on this point, but it is not sufficient to respect the Defence's rights. So what I would propose is that we would proceed, but the reservation is that the Defence has not been able to give all the details to General Galic, whatever the content of the information sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is willing to give some time to the Defence to discuss the matter with General Galic. If it is just minor changes, and I do understand that in most of the cases through, then, of course, it might not be too difficult to prepare. I also do understand that in one issue there is a more important change. If we adjourn until a quarter to 12.00, that would mean that you have some 18 minutes and let's then see whether we can deal, at least, with the minor changes. If the change that would take more time is not solved in an acceptable way for you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber then would like to know what we are actually talking about. We are not that much interested to go through the whole document and hear the evidence, but if there is the remaining issue, something that is really of importance, we will then get more information on that and see what we should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. The Defence would like to ask for half an hour that is, until noon, so that we can read the document through and then, of course, we would have to translate it, and I would have to do it, and I would need some time. And also, we would have to discuss this with General Galic and the three of us will have to confer, obviously, including Madam Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. May I also take it that if we have half an hour now, that the chance that we would have to take a second break would be smaller and that there is a fairer chance that we could continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence will try and do this in quarter of an hour, 20 minutes. I apologise, but I really cannot do interpreting or translation so quickly into Serbian, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well then we will give you a bit more time than you asked for. We will adjourn until five minutes to 12.00 so that we will have at least some --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. --- Break taken at 11.30 a.m

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises that you had to wait for 10 additional minutes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is the Defence ready to start the cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less, Mr. President, yes. And what I wanted to say, thank you for giving us the time that was necessary for us. We have resolved the problem with General Galic but simply, I had organised it in such a way to -- for the hearing to last for four or four and-a-half hours that the Prosecution said it would last, examination would last that long. And we tried to reorganise and we believe that it may take a little more time for this reason. We are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution took one hour and 20 minutes, and let's see where we come in that time. And if it would not be sufficient, we will then have to see. Of course, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you also know that granting extra time might also depend on the way you use the time which is available for you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Abdel-Razek, good morning. I will ask you certain questions. As much as possible, General, I would like to ask you to answer with a "yes" or a "no" if that is possible, in order to gain time. Thank you. General, could you tell us, first of all, why did General MacKenzie stop working at his post?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Relevance, Mr. President. It predates the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it precedes, but not very much and I would like to remind you that one of the positions of the Prosecution was to say that there was a campaign in place before General Galic came to take up his position, and that we would need to go back to that period before General Galic took up his post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. It might have some relevance but, of course, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it depends on your next questions whether this becomes apparent or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Is the question still -- [In English] As a matter of fact, [Interpretation] I will speak in Arabic. Actually, I do not know why General MacKenzie left the sector, however, I received a letter while I was in Angola, asking me to take over the Sarajevo Sector as a successor to Mr. MacKenzie, who was asked to join his country. That is the letter I received while I was working in Angola. However, as to the "why," I do not know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for your answer. Do you know if these reasons were political?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if the witness says that he doesn't know the "why," you can't ask him whether the reasons were political or family reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I agree with you. I was only listening to the French booth and I am looking at the transcript now. The French booth was saying the exact reason, and I thought the exact reason would make it so so that there was a general Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reason, of a different reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just verify with the French booth that the answer was translated as that the General did not know the precise reasons, while the English translation is that the witness would not know the reasons why.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fact, the French booth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... perhaps after the French and the English interpreters have conferred. Yes, well, you may put your next question. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. My following question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not very precise. You may repeat your question you just put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you know in general any reason why General MacKenzie left, that is, do you know in general if these reasons had a political character?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I would ask you to believe me, I do not know. However, as a military man, I received an order to go to Sarajevo and assume responsibility for this sector. And I do not know why MacKenzie left the sector. And even when I arrived, I did not see him there. He has already departed. So I am not aware of the reasons why he left. Maybe his mandate or his function ended. I do not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to ask you about the situation of destruction, the destructions that occurred in the city, that occurred in the city at the time of your arrival. Could you confirm, General, if that is possible by a "yes" or "no," whether most of the destructions, material destructions of buildings, occurred along the line of the demarcation line, the confrontation line which was separating the two warring parties?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: It was possible to see in a clear way, and this is not a private view but it is the view of anyone who were witness to what happened in Sarajevo. Whole buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, General, could you perhaps be a little more precise? My question was: If most of the destruction occurred in the area along the confrontation line, that is, where the parties were facing each other?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, I would like to ask you some questions on military targets in Sarajevo. Could you tell us, General, today where the brigades were located in Sarajevo, what their names were, please? Not what their names, but how many, the number of them.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I do not recall these details, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know, General, at the time of your mandate in Sarajevo, where exactly were located the headquarters of each of the numerous brigades in Sarajevo? I mean you personally, did you know then?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Not the brigades. I knew their positions on the map. I knew the main headquarters where the most important persons are positioned, namely, the main headquarters. I know their location, but as for the minor units, I do not recall their specific positions. I used to know their position on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you a number of questions that will follow each other, and I would like you to tell me if you know these names. If any of these names mean anything to you, then I would ask you to stop me and tell me what they are. I will start. General, do you know the following names: Sultan Fatih, Fatih, Kobra, Ljiljana, Boris and Drago Prazina, Zulfikar, Crni Labudovi, Black Swans, Silver Fox, Akrepi, Mudris, Dedo, Delta? Do any of these names meaning anything to you?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I will continue with other names: Gras, Pavle Goranin, Petar Dakic, Kulin Ban, Caco, Celo.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: If you allow me, can I comment on these names, sir. When I meet with people, I meet with specific persons and those persons are accompanied by other persons, however, I deal with the person concerned. As a commander, I do not recall the names of other persons accompanying the General Galic, for example. I know that he comes with a number of persons, but I do not know their names. I do remember some names, but not the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you know a name, please indicate so. If you don't know the name or don't remember the name -- Did you hear the last names mentioned to you, that was Gras, Pavle Goranin, Petar Dakic, Kulin Ban, Caco, Celo? I think that is what we have in the transcript, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would add the name of Juka. Does this name mean anything to you, Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. General, do you know, please, where this person called Juka Prazina had his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I did not use to deal with this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, it is possible not to have contact with someone, but still know where this person is. Should I conclude that you did not know where his headquarters, his military headquarters, was?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I don't know anything about his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if I -- if I dare ask you in a general way, do you know if his headquarters were located either on the ground floor or perhaps on the first floor of a building?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Which building do you refer to, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I am talking about buildings that could have been used by such-and-such a company or such-and-such a brigade, if you ever visited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. In spite of the fact that the witness has said, "I don't know anything about his headquarters," my learned colleague persists. He has not asked the witness whether indeed this person Juka had headquarters. And in his last question he continues to refer --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps as a general rule, I might have the right to speak without being interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just intervene. I take it, listening to the French - and I think that is the only thing that Mr. Piletta-Zanin was asking our attention for - that the issue you raised might be the result of a translation problem since I did understand that Mr. Piletta-Zanin was not asking about the headquarters of Juka Prazina but in general about the existence of his headquarters. I would not allow someone to interrupt. Perhaps we could find a code that if someone says, one of the parties, "translation," that he indicates that the whole issue entirely rests upon perhaps a translation problem. And under these circumstances, I would allow an interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have not only yellow papers but, yes, as kind of a red sign. I think we could agree on that. Would you then please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just say one thing: I do not blame Mr. Ierace for asking not to be interrupted, neither do I blame you for the way you interrupted under these circumstances. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in a general sense, for different HQs that you may have known, did you see, yes or no, if, as a general rule, generally speaking, these headquarters were either located on the ground floor or on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: The headquarters where I used to meet with Mr. Siber was on the first floor. On the first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you have any knowledge about any other headquarters that you may have visited?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I know the headquarters of Mr. Mustafa something Rajlova [as interpreted], I don't recall. I know that headquarters very well. It is also located on the first floor on one of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the name of the street was? Could you perhaps tell us that?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I am afraid not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will go on to another subject. During your stay in Sarajevo, did you know where weapons factories were located, ammunition factories, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you know if such factories existed, ammunition and weapons manufacturing factories?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: No. It wasn't of any concern to me, did not interest me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you ever take part in investigations following shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: What do you mean by investigations? There weren't any investigations concerning this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when shellings happened, they occurred in the city, you then did not take steps, investigative steps, or investigations to find out where the shelling has come from?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: We used to receive reports from the military observers and we knew from where the shelling came, and we used to send reports to the headquarters in Zagreb. And when the shelling was intense, I do not recall that there was a fact-finding mission or an investigating mission that was entrusted with the task of following up this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, you are therefore saying, if I have understood you correctly, that in order to determine where the fire was coming from, you were basing yourselves only, it seems, on the work done by the observers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only means which helped us to identify the source of the shelling. Sometimes our contact was obstructed and sometimes we were not able to operate in a good way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the quality of the observers was so high, was so good, that they were able to -- you could rely on their word?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Obviously, that was the only available means and it is a common practice in the United Nations, we rely on the reports from the observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with the assistance of Madam Usher, I would like to ask to have the General submitted document number D131. D131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the document has been admitted into evidence under seal, so if --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. I think it should be shown now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to turn into closed session, first, because we have not all with us this document. So it should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- put on the ELMO. We will then turn into closed session for a while dealing with this document. Unfortunately, the public gallery have to leave. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I have to wait until we are back in open session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As you know, the Chamber is very much concerned about the public gallery of the court hearing. Could we please open the public gallery again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know when we are going to have the next break, given the time that we are wasting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps this would be a suitable moment, we then have a short break. And keeping in mind that we had an extra break of half an hour, I would rather limit it now to a quarter of an hour, so that we can see whether we can finish at least the cross-examination of this witness by a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President. THE COURT: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I apologise for raising my voice earlier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't follow you but I think everyone will understand why you did it, and that's what I already tried to express. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, before we go on to other topics, I would like to ask you a question in relation to your rank. You said at one moment that you did become a General in 1992, and in another moment, you said that this rank was given to you in 1995. Just so that we can be very clear on this matter, when did you become a General, please?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Normally, a Brigadier is described as a General. And in English, we say "Brigadier General." But when you become a full General, then you are talking about a Major General. When I was in Sarajevo, I was a Brigadier General, and this is officially confirmed. But then I became a Major General in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So in 1992 you were a Brigadier General, so you were a Brigadier General, General of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So, General, I would like us to go back to your last answer. You said that the municipalities of Ilijas, Ilidza and Grbavica were shelled but that there were military targets there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the military targets that you were thinking of?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I do not have a specific recollection. However, when I used to go to Ilidza on my way to Kiseljak or when I used to go to Ilidza, I could see the remaining of the attacks. I could see the effects or the impact of the shelling on these places. This I can testify to. You can see the impact of bombs and the demolished houses and the marks of the destruction around Sarajevo and inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, in relation to the three areas that I have just mentioned to you, you stated that there were military objectives in them. I might try to be of assistance to you. When you speak of military objectives or targets, did you think possibly of mobile targets such as troops or military vehicles that were likely to move about?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: According to my recollection, for example, there was the headquarters, the command headquarters in Isakovic, which is a village or one of the cities of Sarajevo within the area of Sarajevo, and in that place, there was a military unit moving about the area. We used to see troops, vehicles, and armoured vehicles moving around that area. That is specifically what I meant. In civilian areas, there were military positions. And we also used to see some tanks in those areas where there were fighting or shelling. We could see the marks of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what you are saying in relation to the presence of the soldiers, does that apply to the three municipalities that I have mentioned, Ilijas, Ilidza, Grbavica? But does it also apply to the rest of Sarajevo; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Am I to understand your answer as follows: As being the fact that the people from Sarajevo, they are sometimes called the Presidency Army, that they had a large number of heavy artillery, such as mortars? Can you answer with a yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I don't understand the concept of President's Army or Presidency Army. I have not heard this concept before. However, I can state that they used to have mortars, and those were one of the problems I raised with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What I meant by "Presidency Army," the people from Sarajevo and not the people around Sarajevo. In other words, they are also sometimes called the Muslims. Looking at the words you used to qualify mortars, do we also think or mention heavy mortars?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: No. Mortars, low calibre, not the heavy ones, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you know whether the so-called Sarajevo forces had what is called multiple rocket launchers?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I haven't heard about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether these same forces had trucks that had been transformed so as to enable transporting and shooting, from the flatbed, mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I did know that they used to position mortars on semi-trucks and they used to operate from various positions and they used to launch their shots from there. And this was one of the problems when we had the firing and shelling around the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely regarding the mortar shelling --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I want to tell Madam Registrar already that we would like to submit part of Exhibit 140 to the witness in a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the mortar shelling, General, do you know whether on various occasions the Sarajevo forces moved closer to the PTT building, among other places, so as to launch attacks towards the outside of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Is it direct to me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it is a question I am putting to you, General.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: As I explained earlier on, are you intending to submit a document on that or can I give you an answer straight away? I was in the UN premises. I used to hear sometimes, I used to hear mortar shelling from very close distance, close distance to the building. And I -- when I asked questions about that, I knew that some of the vehicles were coming from the Muslim part. Some of these vehicles used to shell their fire near the PTT building and they leaved to depart straight away, and apparently that was the tactic used then. I was very violent with them because I raised this issue with Mr. Ganic, Colonel Siber. I told them: "You were shelling and we received the hits back on your behalf." So this is the normal use of the mortars on vehicles, mobile mortars. They used to launch their shots from an area surrounding the PTT, whereas it was prohibited to use the perimeter of the PTT building or within the 500 radius of the UN headquarters. That was prohibited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We have a slight problem with the French booth. One should pay attention to what was said on line 47, 48; the translation is not quite accurate. This being said, General, these mobile mortars, technically speaking, could they have directed their fire onto the city or onto some parts of the city?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: What I received, I did not know who was shooting at whom, but as far as I knew, the PTT building was a target of intensive shelling. And I tried -- when I tried to investigate, I knew that there were some mobile mortars operating nearby, and generally, this happens in the darkness of night. So these mobile vehicles used to shell their fire and depart straight away. So obviously we could not investigate the target and, obviously, this was a difficult operation to undertake because of the critical stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this firing onto locations close to positions such as the PTT building, did that aim at provoking a counterbattery fire, as it is called, counterbattery fire?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I cannot see through their mind, but I was trying to depict the situation and that is what I saw. They used to shoot or -- and we received their attacks. So I do not know otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me, General, but in terms of military activity, if somebody opens the fire onto you with a mortar battery, generally speaking, will that not, in times of in conflict, trigger a response which is called a "counterbattery fire"? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the situation which you have just described close to the PTT building may have been repeated as a pattern but closer to other buildings, such as hospitals, for example? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I cannot corroborate that. However, there were movements of mobile mortars and this is the tactic used. Sometimes those small vehicles move in a quick way. They hit one part and then they depart right away in order to avoid a counterattack. So these mobile vehicles used to hit and run in order to avoid a counterattack. However, as for the shooting, we knew that they were nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My question just a moment ago was somewhat different. I asked you this: Technically speaking, do you know whether these mobile mortars could shoot at the city as well?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: And the intensive skirmishes, it is rather difficult for anyone to establish in an accurate way what was happening. Because as a UN staff, we could not move outside. All those who were monitoring the situation were the observers. The military observers were the ones who used to monitor the sources of fire. And this is the only proof we used to get in order to depict the situation within the city and around it or else in the surrounding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if I understood you properly, but I put to you a merely technical question. In theory, technically speaking, could these mortars target the town?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. You can open fire a distance of 500 metres. This is the technical features of the mortar which allows that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. I have a few questions regarding specific military actions. Were you aware of an action called "Jug" action or operation, "Jug" meaning "south" as well? It was an operation conducted by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina called the Sarajevo Army.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I haven't heard about this operation either from the Bosnian side or in the meetings I had with Mr. Galic. I haven't heard about this throughout my stay in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same question regarding the Koverat operation, the "Envelope" operation, in translation.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard about it, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, were you aware of another two operations named "Oxygen" for one of them and "Container" for the other?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know General, whether someone had tried to smuggle gunpowder into bottles which were usually oxygen bottles which were to be sent to hospitals?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I haven't heard about it. There were many allegations or claims from this Serb side to the effect that there were misuse of the relief convoys. And these are the allegations we were faced with. However, the UNHCR was responsible for these issues. There were inspection teams, investigation teams. However, this falls within the framework of the war of words between the conflicting parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, when you stated that you were aware of claims or allegations that the convoys were not used for the initial aim they were destined for, did you think of anything in particular? If so, what?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: There was a misuse of these things. Those were things raised most predominantly by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we are talking about the use of means, do you know whether during your stay in Sarajevo, the press was in any way manipulated?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: As far as this issue is concerned, there were some things that happened. They were sometimes against the United Nations. The press used to criticise us, attack us. They used to mobilise the public opinion against us, saying that our mandate was very weak and our work to the public did not appear to be positive. So we were the object of direct attacks. They used to say that we were people receiving salaries and that is all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. In order to save time, let me ask you this: Do you know Sir Michael Rose, General Sir Michael Rose?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't remember whether you met personally Michael Rose, General Michael Rose?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I do not recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But are you aware of his name?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to tell you, and I don't think this is being challenged, that we have testimony that the press --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I anticipate what my learned colleague is about to put to the witness. In my respectful submission, this is inappropriate. The comment that was made by that witness related to a period a full 12 months after this witness left Sarajevo. And in any event, it is an inappropriate use of the allowance of putting to witnesses what is uncontested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I specifically ask your response as to the difference in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Mr. President. But it is not because today we demonstrated that there were specific things. And I am saying this in front of the witness so I am trying to couch my thoughts in specific terms. We showed that this applied to a specific time. We could also show that the same type of things would intervene, would happen, before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no question that you are not allowed to ask any questions on the subject, but it was on the way that you did it. The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, as far as you know, did or was the media used as a political means of fighting in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK
utterances.text: I do not understand the meaning of your question. The mass media has always a political role to play.
